segments.text: You're gripping a shield, screaming down a hillside toward a shieldwall, and two long curved horns jut off your helmet, cutting the air on either side of your head. The horns catch the firelight. They look terrifying. They look exactly like every painting, every movie poster, every Halloween costume you've ever seen of a Viking. This is the image burned into your head.
A single wrong picture like this can quietly rewrite an entire culture's history in our heads.
So did any Viking ever actually strap on horns before walking into battle?

Here's the belief almost everyone carries around without question: Viking raiders wore horned helmets into combat, the horns curving up from the sides like a bull's. It feels obvious. It's on flags, beer labels, football helmets. But archaeologists digging across Scandinavia for over a century have found remarkably few actual Viking-age helmets at all. Total confirmed helmets from the entire Viking Age, roughly 793 to 1066, that survive with enough of the skull intact to study? You can count them on one hand.

The best-preserved one is the Gjermundbu helmet, dug out of a burial mound in Norway in 1943, dated to around the year 970. It has a rounded iron cap, a spectacled guard curving over the eyes and nose, and absolutely nothing where horns would attach. No sockets. No rivet holes shaped for anything curved. Just a plain iron dome built to deflect a sword, not to look dramatic.

Why trust one helmet? Because it isn't alone. Fragments from Tjele in Denmark and a handful of other sites all show the same story: plain iron, sometimes mail hanging to protect the neck, occasionally a nose guard. Historian Roberta Frank, who spent years tracing this myth through Old Norse literature, found zero contemporary written descriptions of horned battle helmets either. Not one saga. Not one carving from the era mentions warriors fighting in horns.

So where do actual horned helmets in museums come from, if not the Viking Age? Rewind about two thousand years before the first Viking ship ever launched. In 1942, workers draining a bog near Veksø in Denmark pulled up two bronze helmets, each fitted with long, gently curving horns tipped with little round discs. They're called the Veksø helmets, and they've been dated to roughly 900 to 1100 BCE, the Nordic Bronze Age.

These weren't armor. The bronze is thin, decorative, almost delicate. They were likely worn by a priest or a chieftain in a religious ceremony, maybe alongside sun-worship rituals, definitely not swung into a shield wall. That's over eighteen hundred years separating these horns from the first recorded Viking raid on Lindisfarne in 793. Would you mistake your great-great-great-grandparent's wedding china for something you use in a bar fight? That's roughly the gap we're talking about.

But 19th-century antiquarians didn't always draw that line carefully. Early collectors and popular illustrators, digging through old hoards without modern dating tools, lumped anything old and Nordic into one romantic bucket labeled ancient Norse warrior. A ceremonial priest's headdress from the Bronze Age and a Viking raider a thousand years later got flattened into the same imagined figure. That mistake didn't stay buried in a museum basement. It walked straight onto a stage.

In 1876, composer Richard Wagner's opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen premiered in Bayreuth, Germany. Costume designer Carl Emil Doepler dressed the Norse gods and warriors in flowing furs, winged helmets, and yes, dramatic curved horns. Wagner wanted mythic, larger-than-life figures towering over an audience from the back row of a theater. Historical accuracy wasn't the assignment. Spectacle was.

Why did that image spread so fast? Because it landed inside the Romantic movement, when artists across Europe were painting Norse myth as noble and untamed. Swedish painter Gustav Malmstrom and others had already sketched horned figures decades earlier, but Wagner's production put the look in front of thousands of paying theatergoers at once, night after night. A single stage costume became the visual template every illustrator copied afterward, because it was already proven to work on an audience.

From there it never stopped moving. By the early 1900s, horned helmets showed up on tourist postcards sold in Norway itself. In 1939, cartoonist Alex Raymond drew the horned warrior in his Flash Gordon comics. In 1948, the Minnesota Vikings didn't exist yet, but when the NFL team formed in 1961, they built their whole identity around that same horned image. Have you ever questioned why a football team from Minnesota wears Bronze Age Danish ceremonial gear? Most people never do.

But can we really say never, with total certainty? Here's the honest complication. Most Viking-age helmets we'd expect to find were probably never made of iron at all. Leather, boiled and hardened, wood, and antler don't survive well underground for a thousand years, especially in acidic Scandinavian soil. If a helmet had small horns made from antler lashed on with leather cord, that cord and antler could rot into nothing within a few centuries, leaving no rivet holes, no discoloration, no trace at all. So when archaeologists say no evidence, they mean no surviving evidence. Absence isn't automatically proof of absence. It just means if it happened, it happened in a material that time was never going to let us keep.

So go back to that charge down the hillside, the helmet with two long curved horns catching the firelight. That image didn't come from a Viking battlefield at all. It came from a Bronze Age priest's ritual, borrowed by a German opera designer in 1876, and sold to the entire world ever since. Wagner's costume department gave you a myth so good, so visually perfect, that even a total absence of battle evidence couldn't kill it.

Somewhere in a Norwegian museum, a plain iron dome with a simple eye guard sits under glass, unglamorous, undramatic, and true. Nobody buys a postcard of it. Nobody puts it on a football helmet. Real history is rarely as loud as the myth built on top of it. Next time you see those curving horns on a lunchbox or a mascot, you're not looking at Norse memory. You're looking at a nineteenth-century costume designer's best sales pitch, one that's still working on you today.

hero.hair: short dark-brown cropped hair, solid fill, no highlights (hex #3A2A1F).
hero.outfit: muted forest green short tunic (hex #3B6A44), brown belt (hex #6B4A2A), dark gray wool leggings (hex #5A5A5A), brown boots (hex #6B4A2A).
hero.reasoning: The script follows one persistent visual throughline: the narration repeatedly addresses 'you' as a Viking-charging avatar and returns to that embodied image as the episode's emotional anchor. The investigation is built around that viewer-as-protagonist experiencing the myth and then learning why it is wrong, so a single persistent 'viewer' hero is required.
accessories: Gjermundbu-style iron helmet (for accurate scenes) or theatrical horned helmet (for dramatized fantasy scene only)
hero.bodyProportions: 1 head : 4 torso+legs; limbs thin; no exaggerated musculature.
hero.bodyConstruction: Stick torso and limbs with slightly rounded joints; hands are simple mitten shapes with no individual fingers unless required for close detail (then two-thumb-plus-index lines allowed).
hero.semanticIdentity: viewer_viking — the second-person avatar placed in imagined Viking scenes (the 'you' who charges with horns in the opening).
forbiddenMutations: hair color must never shift from short dark-brown to any other shade
skin tone must not be altered from #ECDCB3
tunic color must not change from muted forest green in Viking-era viewer appearances
authentic iron helmet must never display riveted horn sockets or attached horns
hero.canonicalAppearance: Viewer avatar: a flat 2D stickman constructed with a uniform thin black outline and solid color fills. Head: round stickman head with a simple stick-eye pair (two small black dots) and no mouth by default; hair: short dark-brown cropped hair (solid fill) visible only when helmet is off; skin tone: neutral light tan (hex #ECDCB3). Body: simple stickman torso with shoulders, arms and legs proportioned at roughly 1:4 head-to-body ratio. Outfit (Viking context): a short-sleeved tunic in muted forest green (hex #3B6A44) ending mid-thigh, simple brown belt (hex #6B4A2A), knee-length wool leggings in dark gray (hex #5A5A5A), and simple brown leather boots (solid, no texture). Accessories when shown: round wooden shield (see object entry) strapped to left arm; simple round iron helmet without horns (see Gjermundbu canonical object) when the scene is archaeological/accurate. When the 'myth' version is shown only for the charging fantasy, the viewer avatar wears the theatrical horned helmet (see roleArchetype 'theatrical_horned_helmet' for canonical horned prop) but this is explicitly fictional dramatization. PersistentIdentifyingFeatures: ["short dark-brown cropped hair", "neutral light tan skin (#ECDCB3)", "muted forest green short tunic", "round wooden shield strapped to left arm", "simple stickman construction with thin black outline"]. BodyProportions: "1 head : 4 torso/legs, limbs thin and slightly elongated relative to head (classic stickman proportions)." EmotionalExpressionLanguage: "Uses simple mouth-shape swaps only in closeups: neutral (no mouth), small open circle for shouting/surprise, thin curved line for frown. Eyes remain two dots; eyebrows added as short black strokes when emphasis needed."
hero.headFaceConstruction: Round head, two dot eyes, optional short black stroke eyebrows, hair as solid fill cap when visible.
hero.emotionalExpressionLanguage: Simple iconic mouth/eyebrow swaps: open circle for shouting, thin downward curve for seriousness, raised short stroke brows for surprise.
persistentIdentifyingFeatures: round wooden shield strapped to left arm
simple iron dome helmet (equal spacing of rivets) when shown authentic

world.era: Multiple eras shown distinctly: Viking Age (~793–1066 CE), Nordic Bronze Age (~c. 1800–500 BCE), late 19th century (c. 1800s), and present day.
world.geography: Northern European coastal/woodland palette for Viking/bronze scenes; interior stage lighting vignette for theatre; neutral museum floor for modern scenes.
world.architecture: Simple flattened silhouettes: Viking longship prows and timber longhouse roofs reduced to essential shapes; Bronze Age ritual stones or wooden posts as minimal vertical elements; 19th-century theatre with proscenium arch silhouette; museum with glass cases and panels.
world.weatherTimeConventions: Battle charge: late-afternoon warm rim light vignette (for drama). Digs: overcast neutral daylight. Bronze ritual: sunrise/sunset warm golden wash. Theatre: harsh warm stage spotlights with dark auditorium silhouette. Museum: soft gallery diffuse white light.
world.environmentalColorRules: Use a consistent environment tint per era: Viking scenes—cool desaturated blues/greens; Bronze Age—warmer ochres and muted golds; 19th-century theatre—deep crimson and warm stage ambers; museum—neutral grays and soft white.
historicalScientificConstraints: Viking-age helmets shown as iron domes with nasal/spectacle guards (Gjermundbu-type) and NO attached horns.
Veksø bronze horned headdresses are thin decorative bronze with full horns; show them as ceremonial, not combat armor.
world.recurringEnvironmentConstruction: 3 flat layers per scene: background wash/sky, midground shapes (hills/trees/longship/theatre arch), foreground action with figure silhouettes and props. Keep layer edges clean and geometric.

palette.contrastRules: Keep figure colors mid-contrast against their era background: viewer tunic contrasts with surrounding landscape; authentic iron helmets contrast against warm museum plinths. The theatrical horned helmet uses saturated contrast to signal fictionality.
palette.environmentPaletteRules: Assign palettes by era: Viking—use primary forest green (#3B6A44), neutral iron gray (#4A4A4A), and light tan skin (#ECDCB3). Bronze Age—dominant warm ochres and bronze (#B6782B, #C57B2A) with pale horn highlights (#F2E6D1). Theatre—deep reds (#B22222) and warm amber accents. Museum—neutral pale background (#FFF5E0) and steel-gray display cases (#4A4A4A).

textPolicy.exceptionsPolicy: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

bible.visualTone: playful but evidence-driven: visceral and dramatic in the opening 'you charging' beat, sober and slightly skeptical when examining finds, gently ironic during the Wagner/theatre beat, and quietly corrective in the closer.
negativeRules: painterly, sketchy, or textured drift away from flat solid fills
stickman construction mutating into a more detailed/realistic character mid-episode
shading, gradients, or texture appearing despite the flat-fill policy
Do not depict archaeological evidence that does not exist: never invent a riveted horn socket or a buried horned Viking skeleton.
Do not use the theatrical horned helmet as an example of archaeological proof; it is only a cultural/artistic artifact.

styleContract.detailLevel: Minimal — enough to read instantly at a glance, never busy or cluttered
styleContract.lineLanguage: Uniform thin, clean black outlines of identical weight everywhere; no sketchiness, no variable line weight, no cross-hatching
styleContract.realismLevel: Non-realistic, iconographic — identity is carried by a handful of discrete flat features, never facial realism
styleContract.colorStrategy: Use full color to make era shifts immediately legible: warm ochres for Bronze Age, cool desaturated greens/blues for Viking battle context, warm ambers/reds for theatre, and neutral modern tones for museum/merch. Use the theatrical horned helmet in saturated, slightly cartoonish colors to cue 'not archaeological.'
styleContract.shadingPolicy: None — flat solid fills only, no gradients, no soft shadow rendering, no highlights
styleContract.shapeLanguage: Simple geometric primitives — circles, rounded rectangles, straight or gently curved lines — never intricate or organic detail
styleContract.dimensionality: 2D flat, no 3D rendering, no depth shading, no perspective distortion beyond simple flat-layer staging
styleContract.lightingStrategy: Use stylized, era-specific lighting: dramatic warm rim light for the opening charge; flat, neutral daylight for dig scenes; directional warm spotlights for theatre; soft diffuse gallery light for museum. Lighting is graphic only (no gradients)—implemented by solid-color shapes and hard edges.
styleContract.illustrationStyle: Simplified stickman/doodle explainer construction — circle heads, dot eyes, stick limbs, mitten hands — never a detailed or semi-realistic character
styleContract.backgroundStrategy: 2-3 flat color layers (background/midground/foreground), never a fully rendered or photographic environment
forbiddenStyleTraits: realistic anatomy, fingers, or necks on stickman characters

bible.visualPremise: Flat 2D stickman-explainer visuals that stage a short visual investigation: drop the viewer into imagined Viking-action, cut to archaeological finds, then to Bronze Age ritual objects and 19th-century theatre, and close in a modern museum/merchandise context.

cameraLanguage.framingConventions: Establishing wide shot for the opening charge (viewer foreground, hillside midground, line of enemy silhouettes far background). Cut to medium closeups for artifact inspection (helmet under glass). Use two-up split frames for comparisons. Use inset timeline closeups when naming dates.
cameraLanguage.visualHierarchyRules: Always keep the hero/viewer visually central in 'you' moments. In explanatory beats, center objects (helmet, Veksø) with the archaeologist or curator slightly off-center to the left or right. In theatre beats, stage arch frames the horned-helmet prop and designer.
cameraLanguage.simplicityReadabilityRules: Every frame must read clearly at thumbnail size — avoid busy multi-subject compositions unless the beat's own visual concept specifically requires comparing multiple subjects at once
cameraLanguage.whenEstablishingVsCloseupVsDiagram: Establishing shots set era and mood; closeups for proof (rivets, nasal guard, lack of horn sockets); diagrams/timelines for chronology and for the preservation caveat.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used as the authoritative archaeological counterexample to the horned-helmet myth and shown in museum/archaeology beats.
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Gjermundbu helmet: a plain iron rounded dome with visible rim rivets spaced evenly, a single integrated spectacle-like eye/nasal guard (two cheek flanges joined over the nose area) and no horn sockets or rivet patterns for horn attachments; surface solid flat iron color (hex #4A4A4A). Mounted on a simple foam stand inside a glass case for museum shots.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Illustrates the actual prehistoric source of horned imagery (Bronze Age ritual objects) repeatedly referenced in the narrative.
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Veksø bronze helmet: thin decorative bronze cap with two long gently curving horns attached, horn tips capped with small circular discs. Bronze color warm (hex #B6782B) with pale horn color (hex #F2E6D1). Design reads as ceremonial headdress, not protective armor.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used in the opening charge and recurring historical-context compositions to ground the viewer as a combatant without horns.
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Round wooden shield: solid circular disk with visible stave lines simplified to two or three radial marks, central iron boss (hex #4A4A4A), outer rim banded in darker brown (hex #6B4A2A). Strapped to left arm of viewer and raider archetypes.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Shows the modern spread and persistence of the horned-Viking image in popular culture and merchandise.
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Modern postcard/lunchbox image: stylized dramatic horned-helmet figure in bold saturated colors (deep red background hex #B22222, horned helmet per 'theatrical_horned_helmet'), labeled with a small price tag icon to indicate merch. Must be captioned visually as 'souvenir'.

roleArchetypes.role: the viewer (second-person Viking-era avatar) used in the opening fantasy and in accurate archaeological contrasts.
roleArchetypes.usedFor: All 'you' addresses, the opening charge, and any cutaways that require embodying the misconception.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Viewer avatar: a flat 2D stickman with a round head, two dot eyes, short dark-brown cropped hair (hex #3A2A1F), neutral light tan skin (#ECDCB3), wearing a muted forest green short tunic (hex #3B6A44), brown belt (hex #6B4A2A), dark gray leggings (hex #5A5A5A), brown boots (hex #6B4A2A). Carries a round wooden shield (see object 'viking_shield') on left arm. In accurate scenes wears a plain iron dome helmet (Gjermundbu-style). In the dramatized fantasy only, swaps to the theatrical horned helmet prop (see 'theatrical_horned_helmet') — that swap must be visually flagged as 'fictional/dramatic' (e.g., a small 'stage light' icon or soft vignette).

roleArchetypes.role: a modern archaeologist explaining finds and showing a helmet under glass.
roleArchetypes.usedFor: When narrating archaeological evidence, showing helmet fragments, or giving cautious caveats about preservation.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Flat 2D stickman with short neat black hair (hex #222222), light-medium skin tone (hex #E0C8A8), wearing a short-sleeved pale blue buttoned shirt (hex #A8D0E6), khaki pants (hex #C6B58A), and a folded clipboard or small trowel held in right hand. Glasses optional: simple round black-rim glasses when closeup is needed. Wears a name badge rectangle on chest when speaking authoritatively. Expression typically calm and explanatory.

roleArchetypes.role: a Bronze Age ritual figure to illustrate the Veksø helmets' original ceremonial context.
roleArchetypes.usedFor: All Bronze Age ritual reenactment imagery showing the original context of the horned bronze finds.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Flat 2D stickman wearing a simple knee-length ceremonial robe in muted ochre (hex #C57B2A) with a decorative thin band across the chest (hex #FFDDAA). Headwear: the Veksø-style bronze horned headdress (see object 'vekso_helmet') perched on a simple cloth cap; hands raised in a ritual posture. Skin tone slightly darker than viewer (hex #DDBA93). Constructed as a stylized archetype, not realistic detail.

roleArchetypes.role: 19th-century opera/theatre costume designer and the theatre crowd used to show the origin of the dramatic stage look.
roleArchetypes.usedFor: When describing Wagner's 1876 production and the diffusion of the stage-horn look into popular culture.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Designer: flat 2D stickman with slicked-back dark hair (hex #1F1F1F), small moustache optional, wearing a dark formal frock coat (hex #2B2B2B) and holding an oversized costume sketch. Theatre crowd: simplified stickman silhouettes in period dress (late 19th century) with a soft warm wash vignette.

roleArchetypes.role: modern museum curator/label-placer guiding viewers past a plain helmet under glass and a display of ritual objects.
roleArchetypes.usedFor: Final scenes in museum, the sober contrast between the plain iron helmet and the theatrical horned prop in a display or postcard context.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Flat 2D stickman with medium brown hair in a tidy bun (hex #5A3B2A), wearing a dark navy blazer (hex #243B55) over a cream blouse (hex #FFF5E0) and holding a museum label or pointer. Calm expression, gestures toward display cases.

roleArchetypes.role: modern public / merch user to show postcards, NFL logos, and lunchboxes using the horned image.
roleArchetypes.usedFor: Shots showing the myth's persistence across postcards, team logos, and merchandising.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Generic stickman in contemporary casual clothes: short-sleeve t-shirt in light gray (hex #D6D6D6) and jeans, holding a postcard or a lunchbox with a horned-Viking image.

roleArchetypes.role: generic Viking raider archetype used in quick background shots of raids or shieldwalls (always historically conservative).
roleArchetypes.usedFor: Group combat scenes and background composition where a Viking presence is needed but no individual identity is required.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman wearing a short tunic in muted browns (hex #7B5A3B), carrying an oval or round shield, wearing an iron dome helmet with nasal guard (Gjermundbu-type) and no horns. Used in group scenes (shieldwall) without unique facial detail.

roleArchetypes.role: a prop archetype: the dramatic horned helmet used in fantasy/theatre/advertising shots (explicitly fictional within episode).
roleArchetypes.usedFor: Only in dramatized fantasy sequences, historical-inaccuracy callouts, and examples of postcards/mascots/merchandise — never to represent archaeological evidence.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: A theatrical helmet prop: exaggerated, symmetrical curved horns sweeping upward and outward from a decorative leather or faux-metal cap; horns are solid pale bone color (hex #F2E6D1) with dark metal banding accent (hex #444444). The helmet surface is ornamented with stylized etching. When shown, it must be visually labeled or vignetted as 'stage prop / fictional'.

neverDrift: the recipe's own universal style (flat 2D, uniform outline, flat fills, no shading/gradients/texture)
Never show an authentic Viking (archaeologically accurate) iron helmet with attached horns or riveted horn sockets.
Never change the viewer's canonical tunic color or hair/skin specification.
Never display the Veksø bronze helmet as protective thick armor — always present it as thin, decorative, ceremonial.
allowedToVary: Small accessory swaps (e.g., archaeologist clipboard vs trowel) are allowed.
Background crowd silhouettes in theatre or museum may vary in posture and clothing silhouette, but not in era palette.
episodeWideConsistencyRules: Whenever a horned helmet is shown outside explicit theatrical/ceremonial contexts, visually flag it as 'fictional/stage' (spotlight icon or label).
All archaeological helmets shown as evidence must match the Gjermundbu canonicalDescription when the narration references the Gjermundbu find.

graphicLanguage.colorUse: Uses this episode's own palette (#3B6A44, #4A4A4A, #B6782B, #F2E6D1, #243B55) as flat fills, consistent with narrative scenes — never a separate infographic color scheme.
graphicLanguage.lineStyle: The exact same line weight and fill language as narrative scenes — a graphic must never look like a different visual universe from the story frames around it
graphicLanguage.mapConventions: Minimal map of Scandinavia as a flat silhouette in muted gray with a single bright dot for key find locations (Gjermundbu, Veksø).
graphicLanguage.arrowsConnectors: Simple flat-filled arrow shapes and thin connector lines, same line language as everything else
graphicLanguage.comparisonLayouts: Two-up comparisons: left panel = 'archaeological reality' (Gjermundbu helmet, label, sober palette), right panel = 'popular image' (horned theatrical helmet, saturated palette). Each panel uses the same scale and a short fact-blurb beneath.
graphicLanguage.backgroundBehavior: Clean, uncluttered flat backgrounds (often light/white or the episode's own environment palette) — never assumed to be white-only; the Production Bible's graphic language decides per episode
graphicLanguage.diagramConventions: Timelines are horizontal bands with three labeled ticks: Bronze Age (~1000 BCE), Viking Age (793–1066 CE), 19th century (c. 1800s). Dates use short labels and one-line captions. Use minimal icons (helmet silhouette, theatrical mask, museum case) above ticks.
graphicLanguage.whitespaceBehavior: Generous but not empty — whitespace isolates the one idea a graphic communicates, it is never filler
graphicLanguage.overlayTextBehavior: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.
graphicLanguage.timelineConventions: Simple flat horizontal bar with spaced era-color fills: bronze ochre for Bronze Age, muted green for Viking Age, crimson for 19th-century, cool gray for modern era. Use consistent typographic weight for date numbers.
graphicLanguage.symbolicMetaphorLanguage: Use the 'stage spotlight' icon or small vignette to signal theatrical/fictional sources; use a small magnifying-glass icon for archaeological evidence. Use a dotted-line 'absence' halo to show the lack of surviving organic material when discussing preservation caveat.
graphicLanguage.characterUseInsideGraphics: Stickman characters, objects, and simplified environments are explicitly ALLOWED and encouraged inside a graphic when they clarify the point — a graphic is a composition family, never a text-only template

factualVisualConstraints: Viking-age helmets shown as iron domes with nasal/spectacle guards (Gjermundbu-type) and no horn attachments.
Veksø helmets must be shown as Bronze Age ceremonial thin-bronze headdresses with long curved horns and small disc tips.
No contemporary Viking-age textual or carved depiction of horned battle helmets should be visually suggested in saga/carving cutaways.

v.description: visualConcept: ONE still image, a single frozen moment (max ~15 words).

m.description: motionIntent as 'camera move | subject motion | environment motion', a few words each.

cast.description: subjects on screen; omit if none.

t.description: exact on-screen text (<= 5 words) for SHORT_TEXT; what to render for PROGRAMMATIC.

motif.description: Only on the callback's plant / payoff beat; omit otherwise.

hold.description: HOLD reason (beat may run to 9 s); omit otherwise.

punch.description: PUNCH reason (beat may be under 1.8 s); omit otherwise.
